title: Ezekiel 44:4–14
context: Ezekiel’s guide brings him to the north gate, and Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory filling the house and falls on his face. The LORD tells him, as son of man, to mark carefully the laws of the house and its entrances and exits. Ezekiel is to tell the rebellious house of Israel that their abominations must end: they had brought foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, into the sanctuary to serve, and had not kept charge of the holy things themselves (compare Numbers 3:10; Leviticus 22:25). No such foreigner shall enter the sanctuary. The phrase uncircumcised in heart and flesh joins outward covenant sign and inward devotion (compare Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 9:26), and here it is used within the temple’s holiness rules, not as a statement about the salvation of individual foreigners; elsewhere the prophets welcome foreigners who join themselves to the LORD (Isaiah 56:6–7). The Levites who went astray after idols will bear their iniquity: they will serve as gatekeepers and slaughter offerings for the people, but they will not come near to serve as priests. Interpreters discuss how this relates to the distinction between priests and Levites in Numbers 18:1–7 and to the priests of the high places in 2 Kings 23:9; the text does not settle the history, and readings differ. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s holiness and the seriousness of unfaithful leadership.

verses.text: Then he brought me by the way of the north gate before the house; and I looked, and behold, the LORD’s glory filled the LORD’s house; so I fell on my face.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel brought to the north gate, seeing the LORD’s glory filling the house, and falling on his face. Worship is the fitting response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the glory filling the house as the heart of the vision (compare 43:5). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about awe before God’s presence.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Son of man, mark well, and see with your eyes, and hear with your ears all that I tell you concerning all the ordinances of the LORD’s house and all its laws; and mark well the entrance of the house, with every exit of the sanctuary.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel, as son of man, to mark well the laws and entrances of the house. Careful attention is required.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God regulating access to his presence. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing rules meant to guard the holiness of the sanctuary.

verses.text: You shall tell the rebellious, even the house of Israel, ‘The Lord GOD says: “You house of Israel, let that be enough of all your abominations,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD calling the rebellious house of Israel to end its abominations. The past must not be repeated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God confronting Israel’s history of profaned worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to repentance within the temple vision.

verses.text: in that you have brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to profane it, even my house, when you offer my bread, the fat and the blood; and they have broken my covenant, to add to all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD rebuking Israel for bringing foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, into the sanctuary to profane it. The covenant was broken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the joining of outward sign and inward devotion (compare Deuteronomy 10:16). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in its temple-holiness frame.

verses.text: You have not performed the duty of my holy things; but you have set performers of my duty in my sanctuary for yourselves.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying Israel had not kept charge of his holy things but set others in its place. Responsibility was neglected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see failure to guard God’s sanctuary as a serious offense. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against careless worship.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says, “No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter into my sanctuary, of any foreigners who are among the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the rule that no foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh shall enter the sanctuary. Holiness governs access to God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rule within the temple’s holiness laws, not as a verdict on individual foreigners (compare Isaiah 56:6–7). Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But the Levites who went far from me when Israel went astray, who went astray from me after their idols, they will bear their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites who went astray after idols bearing their iniquity. Unfaithfulness carries real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God holding leaders accountable for leading others astray. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame, holding the details of the history with care.

verses.text: Yet they shall be ministers in my sanctuary, having oversight at the gates of the house, and ministering in the house. They shall kill the burnt offering and the sacrifice for the people, and they shall stand before them to minister to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites still serving as gatekeepers and slaughtering offerings for the people. Discipline does not mean total rejection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see mercy mixed with judgment in the Levites’ continued service. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God still uses those he disciplines.

verses.text: Because they ministered to them before their idols, and became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I have lifted up my hand against them,” says the Lord GOD, “and they will bear their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD lifting his hand against the Levites because they ministered before idols and caused Israel to stumble. Leaders bear greater responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gravity of leading God’s people into sin. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober warning to all who serve in worship.

verses.text: They shall not come near to me, to execute the office of priest to me, nor to come near to any of my holy things, to the things that are most holy; but they will bear their shame and their abominations which they have committed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites barred from priestly service and the most holy things, bearing their shame. Their access is limited.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the consequences of unfaithfulness in the restriction of their role. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in its temple setting, without extending it beyond that frame.

verses.text: Yet I will make them performers of the duty of the house, for all its service and for all that will be done therein.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD still making the Levites keepers of the house for all its service. There is a place for them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision of a role even after failure. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s house needs every kind of faithful service.
